en: The Ritual for the Offering of Food from the Essentials of Yoga Practice (*Yogācārabhūmi-saṃgraha-bali-vidhi*).

(Now, those who wish to universally make offerings and provide universal relief should, with sincere and utmost devotion, adorn the ritual arena and prepare, according to their means, incense, flowers, food, drink, pure water, and so forth. Having done so, one should perform the offering during the hours of the Dog or the Pig; thus the hungry ghosts shall obtain food.)

The donor obtains merit. If one lets the appointed time pass, it is merely a waste of energy and provides no benefit for the task at hand; this is derived from the fundamental teachings and is not a mere personal opinion. Should there now be those who violate this, local unrest will ensue—this is precisely the fault.

If you wish to understand the underlying reasons in depth, please consult the subsequent commentary, where the text is fully elucidated. (When the assembly has gathered and settled, the praises are recited).
As the incense in the burner is first ignited, the entire Dharma-realm is perfumed; throughout the ocean-like assemblies of Yoga, all hear it from afar as auspicious clouds form in every place.
As our sincere devotion grows ever more earnest, the Buddhas manifest their complete bodies.
Yunlaiji Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva (three times).
This single offering of incense does not descend from heaven, nor does it spring from the earth. Before the two polarities were yet distinguished, its root and source filled all space;
as soon as the single breath of the triple world was divided, its branches and leaves spread throughout the ten directions, transcending the sun and moon.
Its radiance surpasses the exquisite beauty of mountains and rivers. It is simultaneously precept, concentration, and wisdom; it is neither wood, nor fire, nor smoke.

When gathered, it is contained within a single minute atom; when dispersed, its fragrance universally permeates the entire Dharma-realm. As it burns within the incense burner, I offer it with single-minded devotion as an act of pure worship.
To the eternally abiding Triple Gem; to the myriad spirits of the ocean of lands; to the ancestral masters of successive generations; to all the assembly of holy ones;
and to all classes of beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—whether hidden or manifest, sacred or mundane—we universally offer this true incense in common worship.
Gandhameghaśrī Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva (three times).
The Buddha’s face is like the pure, full moon; It is also like a thousand suns emitting radiance.
His halo shines universally throughout the ten directions, Fully endowed with joy, equanimity, compassion, and kindness.
Homage to the Triple Gem of the Buddhas, Dharmas, and Saṅghas of the past, present, and future, as vast as empty space and pervading the Dharma-realm.
Homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Who Ascends the Jewel Throne (three times).
I humbly submit that, having ascended the seat of Yoga, manifesting both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings, one cultivates the Six Perfections in unison;
opening the gate of saving beings and benefiting life, one bestows the three altars equally. With a mind of profound stillness, the entire body is the Great Compassionate King;
as the three karmas respond, the whole being becomes the syllable *Hrīḥ*. If it is truly thus, then cause and effect do not transcend one’s own mind.

Benefiting oneself and others has nothing to do with external things. One can transform a drop of water into the ghee and curd of a long river, and change a morsel of food into the grain-measures of the great earth;
in an instant, one universally relieves the hunger of the world, and in a mere moment, one brings benefit to as many beings in the realm of hungry ghosts as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
If you can understand it in this way, you must universally benefit all sentient beings according to their capacities.
If this were not yet the case, I could not help but proclaim once more these sublime verses:
The Way is the Great Jewel Flower King Throne, Universally protected and sustained by humans and devas; The place where I now ascend to expound it— Wherever the eye touches, that is itself Bodhi.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Great Compassion (At the conclusion of the assembly’s recitation, the practitioner offers this prayer for the water):
As for this water, its eight virtues arise spontaneously from the Dharma-nature. First, it washes away the defilements of the karma of sentient beings;

then, it pervades the Flower Treasury World-realm of Vairocana. Within this realm, there is nowhere that it does not transcend and immerse. Water does not wash water; it is the ultimate subtlety of the Dharmakāya.
Dust does not defile dust; it returns to become one's own self. The vessel-world is eliminated and the ritual site is purified. Sprinkling upon withered trees, they encounter spring once more;
cleansing the defiled lands, they become pure realms. As it is said: "Within, without, and in between, there is no turbidity or filth;
the holy and the ordinary, the hidden and the manifest, are all cool and serene. (The teachings contain secret mantras; one should respectfully recite them.)
(The assembly recites the Great Compassion Mantra in unison. After it is finished, the ritual master [biaobai] intones:
Amṛtarāja Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (three times).
(Attendant Baiyun said: "What is the Brahma-sound?
How does one, regarding this sutra, ultimately reach the other shore? We pray that the Buddha will reveal its subtle and profound mysteries and speak extensively for the sake of all sentient beings.

The Mantra of the Pure Dharma-realm (When reciting the mantra, subdue body and mind; visualize the two syllables Oṃ and Āḥ at the crown of the head and the navel, respectively, in order to bring about purification).
To symbolize the perfection of merit and wisdom: Oṃ raṃ.
Oṃ raṃ oṃ raṃ svāhā. This is the mantra for sprinkling and purifying.
(When reciting this mantra, use the ring finger of the right hand to take up perfumed water, sprinkle it into the air, and smear it upon the palms; then visualize the maṇḍala.)
[Make both the internal and external entirely pure].
Oṃ amoghasiddhi-māyā-svāhā. [This is the mantra for empowering flowers and rice.
When reciting the mantra, hold flowers and rice in the hands; three times, visualize them as seeds of light from which gold, silver, and lapis lazuli are produced.]
Oṃ vajrapuṣpe āḥ hūṃ. (This is the mantra for consecrating the bell and vajra with clouds of precious jewels.
When reciting the mantra, hold flowers and rice in the hands and sprinkle them over the bell and vajra, visualizing them as the seeds of wisdom.)
Oṃ vajrasattva hūṃ | Oṃ vajra kaṭa ha hūṃ | Oṃ ha hūṃ (Recite while holding the vajra and shaking the bell).
I now shake the bell and the vajra; its sound pervades the ten directions. I pay homage and invite all the sages and worthies to come together to this assembly.
This is the vajra held in the hands of all the Tathāgatas.
Vajrayoginī of Great Heroic Awareness, I too shall constantly uphold [you].
May you extinguish the great ignorance of sentient beings. Oṃ hara hara hūṃ (three times).
With her left hand she holds a subtle bell of the seven precious jewels; its great sound vibrates throughout the ten directions and the three times.
The Brahma-voice, clear and resonant, startles and awakens the hearts of demonic adversaries; It shatters and destroys all malevolent sprites, *māra*s, and ghostly specters.
In his right hand he holds the Vajra-pestle for subduing demons, Its majestic power weighing eighty-four thousand *jin*.
It crushes and destroys the celestial and non-celestial hosts of Māra’s retinue, Causing them all to turn their light back upon themselves in yearning devotion.
May all internal and external enemies, māras, the three poisons, and the four harms;
curses, sorcery, Pāpīyān, and the non-Buddhists’ triple-pointed fire-wheels that dispel demons and transform space—may these be made to utterly abandon their inverted dreams and delusions.
May the wrathful celestial māras of the eight directions and four quarters hear me perform this rite, listen attentively, and accept it with faith.
The Secret and Sublime Gāthā of Jambhala: A Fingernap to Sweep Away Evil and Malevolent Spirits;
The Dharani of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. Oṃ jātamaraduḥkhapravāhaduḥkhanirghātaṃ kuru svāhā.

The Master raises the Five-Buddha Crown. The assembly recites the Cundī Dhāraṇī three times.)
The Great Majestic Power of the Five Buddhas of the Five Directions, Boundaries sealed and demons subdued throughout the atoms of all lands;
Tonight, they manifest upon the crown of Vairocana— A single gaze, a single prostration, and all return to the Truth.
Vairocana Tathāgata, compassionate empowerment (Recite while taking flowers and rice with the right hand):
I and all sentient beings within the realm of phenomena, from this moment forth until we have realized enlightenment,
vow to take refuge in the Vajra Master and the Three Jewels.
Namo Guru-vajraye | Namo Buddhāya | Namo Dharma-ye | Namo Saṃghāya ||
Oṃ lili hahaha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ oṃ śrī mahākāla hahaha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ a hūṃ | (Taking the flowers and rice held in hand,
scatter them into the expanse of space; imagine that the falling precious grains all become clouds of flower and incense offerings.)
(Strike the sounding board.
Arranged are fragrant flowers upon the established jewel altar; The myriad realms of the Buddhas reside upon the tip of a single hair.
The mind merges with the subtle principle, making empty space small; The Way accords with True Suchness, making the Dharma-realm vast.
The marks and signs of his compassionate body are like the full autumn moon; where his transformation bodies soar, the evening clouds gather thick.
Within the mass of incense smoke, we behold his manifestations: Śākyamuni Tathāgata, who contains all myriad phenomena within the ocean-seal; may he bear witness to our merit. (Chorus joins.)
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, secretly bestow your protective grace (congregation joins).
Venerable Ānanda, manifesting expedient means to initiate the teaching (congregation joins; ring the bell while reciting).
The nature-verse on the skillful means of the indestructible essence of self-nature:
The indestructible vajra, the great heroic consciousness, supreme and peerless, with characteristics that transcend all; May all that is now performed be accomplished.

The nature of supreme wisdom is profoundly deep; The sound of the preaching of the most excellent Wheel of Dharma, Through the skillful means of manifesting a body of non-arising— May these deeds now performed cause me to attain the Pure Grounds. (Verse)
May all the ground in every direction— devoid of rubble, sand, and gravel—
become a floor of lapis lazuli as level as the palm of a hand; may it be soft, subtle, and wondrous,
remaining stable like the adornments of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, with a ground of exquisite jewels upon which various flowers bloom.
May gardens, groves, and ponds be without lack; by the sound of the Great Dharma, may they be fully perfected.
May they manifest from the supramundane, composed of various kinds of the seven treasures, with immeasurable light illuminating all places. May all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas dwell therein in peace.
Musical Mantra:
Oṃ vajra-kandhe raṇa raṇa pra-raṇa pra-raṇa sa-pra-raṇa sa-pra-raṇa sarvabhaiṣajya.
OṂ TRĪLOKAVIJAYĀMBHAKA-TRĪNIKA-PARAMĀNTAKARADŪTABHIḤ SARVATĀRMA-GHRĪDĀYA SAṂTRASANA-KARI HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. (Place the bell on the table.)
The King of the Six-Syllable Great Illuminator— his meritorious achievements are immeasurable—
is proclaimed with one voice by the assembly of pure beings present before him: OṂ MUNI MAṆI HŪṂ (recite this together one hundred and eight times).

Regarding the introductory text: phenomena do not arise in isolation; they are produced only by relying upon conditions. The Way does not travel in vain; it responds immediately when meeting with the right circumstances.
Now, as we arrange the flower altar and propagate the Buddha-work, precious incense is burned, sending up clouds and mists of five colors, and candles bloom...
The golden lotus shines like the stars and constellations across the heavens; the music of the Dharma plays the melody of non-arising. The Brahma-sound expounds the most supreme school;
one takes refuge in the five eyes and six supernormal powers, and invites forth the thousands of sages and myriad saints. Thus, the King of Awakening dwells in the world.
He benefited sentient beings through the Dharma; there was no other cause or condition by which he could establish a formal model for others.
Thus, when the Venerable Ānanda was practicing meditative concentration in the forest, he saw at night a king of ghosts whose mouth spat flames and whose hair on the crown of his head emitted smoke.

His physical form was hideous and foul, and his limbs and joints made sounds like those of a broken cart. The fires of hunger blazed within him, and his throat was as narrow as the point of a needle. Witnessing this strange and extraordinary sight, [he reflected...]
The questioner asked, "What is his name? He replied, "His face is aflame. Within three days, you shall fall into my own class.
Ānanda was struck with terror and sought refuge with the Great Awakened One, the Compassionate Honored One. He recounted the preceding causes and requested the method for rescuing him from suffering.

The Buddha bestowed profound and vast expedient means for his benefit and salvation, enabling him to extend his years and increase his lifespan. By reciting the sublime mantras of majestic power, he caused the hungry ghosts—
To provide sustenance, the Dharma-food of ambrosia is bestowed. For empowerment, one must focus single-mindedly on divine mantras; for solemn protection, one must rely upon the rituals of the altar.
Although the invocation occurs but for a moment, the Dharma is transmitted for a thousand ages. When the Golden Mountain is constructed, it shines with natural brilliance without needing a lamp;

when the *māgha* offerings are presented, they pervade the entire Dharma-realm. If there were no spiritual efficacy, how could this have been transmitted through antiquity and the present? Such is its merit.

Only now is it fit to be expounded. Where the Brahma-voice resounds, it reaches upward to the peak of existence; when the Tang-era phonology proclaims it, it extends downward to the limits of the wind-circle.
To clarify the sacred principles, I have thus set forth these words. When the Buddha’s work is completed, all return to the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
As the verse says:
The Tathāgata, Sovereign King of Supreme Radiance, Expounded this wondrous and immeasurable teaching.
In the past, out of joy, I was struck with fear; Due to the "Flaming Mouth" and "Thunderous Sound" rites, I suffered calamity.
I prostrated with utmost sincerity before the Teacher of the World, And earnestly requested the means to bring forth compassion, save all beings, and benefit living creatures.
Now, drawing upon antiquity, I bring this forth once more: Ordinary beings and sages alike traverse the field of liberation.
(Take the ring finger of the right hand and sprinkle scented water over the maṇḍala.)

Oṃ vajrodaka āḥ hūṃ. (Recite this mantra once. Draw a circular mandala once.

Oṃ vajra pūmaya hūṃ. (While reciting this mantra, take flowers and rice with the right hand three times.
Then, taking flowers and rice with both hands, place them upon the maṇḍala and scatter them while circling to the right, like rain falling from the sky. (Cakravāḍa Mountains;
Cakravāḍa Iron Mountains)

the adamantine foundation, by means of the syllable HŪṂ, provides protection.

Oṃ haṃ meru-vināma (Great Sumeru Mountain). Oṃ haṃ śakrasya meru-vināma (Small Sumeru Mountain).

oṃ vaṃ kuruvideha-dvīpa (the continent of Aparagoyānī);

Oṃ śrī-mate-vajra-kurucara-nadaka-malaye samyak-tadan-āvak-phasa-na-karaye hūṃ namaḥ. (When reciting this mantra:)

Place the flower-rice upon the maṇḍala and scatter it into the sky. Visualize that as the precious rice falls, it completely transforms into various palaces, groves, ponds, parasols, canopies, banners, pennants, garments, necklaces, wish-fulfilling jewels, and all manner of ornaments, falling like rain from the sky in an unceasing stream.
With these, make offerings to the Guru and the Three Jewels. Then, taking the flower-rice with your hand from within the central circle, scatter it into the sky while reciting:
"All varieties of offering substances possessed by gods and humans..."
Oṃ sarvadharmagatānāṃ amoghapāśa-mahāvidyārājñī-spharaṇasamayasvāhā hūṃ. (Bind the mudrā and recite the mantra.)

Oṃ sarvadharmagatāḥ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ oṃ vajrābhiseka hūṃ (flower,
light red in color). Oṃ vajra-dhūpa abhiṣeka hūṃ (incense, yellow in color).

Emptiness. Within emptiness, upon the moon disc of one’s own mind, visualize the yellow syllable *ṭraṃ* emitting light that benefits all sentient beings. The light returns to the syllable *ṭraṃ*, which in a single instant transforms into the yellow Buddha Ratnasaṃbhava, his hands forming the mudrā of generosity (*varada-mudrā*).
This constitutes the completion of the non-dual unity. In a single instant, it transforms into a jewel lattice (*ratnajāla*). When using it, cause the lattice to manifest.
The Jewel Lattice Mantra (while reciting the mantra, visualize inexhaustible divine wish-fulfilling jewels emerging from within the lattice and offering them).
Oṃ smara smara mimānaskara mahācakra hūṃ svāhā.

(While the Master recites this mantra, he holds the jeweled casket with his left hand and takes up rice and wine with his right hand; he visualizes that wish-fulfilling jewels fall upon the jeweled casket.)
[The Mantra for Expelling Māras]: Oṃ saptadharaṇi hūṃ.

[Form the mudrā with both hands making vajra-fists, backs of the hands pressed together, the two little fingers hooked together, and the two index fingers extended straight upward; bind the seal at the heart and visualize...]
[From] the hand-seal (*mudrā*), flames emerge to expel the demons of the objective realm (*viṣaya-māra*).
Oṃ vajrāmṛtakuṇḍali hana hana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra for expelling demons (with the two hands crossed outward;
the two index fingers extended straight upward; forming the seal at the chest; moving the hands like a fan; from the seal, flames emerge, thereby expelling all demons).
Oṃ vajra-ghāṭa hūṃ. (The mantra for expelling māras:
Interlace the two hands with palms facing upward. Form the mudrā before you and visualize vajra-flames radiating from within the seal, causing the māras to depart.)
Oṃ vajrasattvānala-hata-paca-marda-bhañja-rana hūṃ phaṭ. (The Mantra of the Seal of True Emptiness:
Interlace the two hands with palms facing inward; extend the thumbs, ring fingers, and middle fingers straight upward. Recite the mantra.)
Oṃ svabhāva-śuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāva-śuddho ’haṃ. Contemplate within emptiness.

Washing the feet with flower-fragrance, lamps, ointments, food, and music— pure, transparent, and unimpeded—
like the various clouds manifested by Samantabhadra gathering for offering, filling the void and pervading the Dharma-realm, continuing without interruption until the end of saṃsāra.
(Form the mudrās and recite the mantras.)

Raraṇa-svabhraraṇa-svabhraraṇa-sarvavittātikrāntapralambamaho-pranijā-parāmṛṣṭanādasupaviśva-tarima-hṛt.

Tadhye dharmadhātusvabhāva-niruttara-jñāna-pratītyasamutpāda-mahāśvara-maṇaye svāhā | Oṃ āḥ hūṃ (Recite three times. Then,
having finished scattering the flowers and rice, ring the bell and recite:)
Visualize clearly the pure and vast maṇḍala, Filled with the four continents and immeasurable jewels and precious gems,
Each like a mass of *maṇi* jewels as high as Mount Sumeru; I offer this to the Guru and the Triple Gem— may you remain in peace.
The Maṇḍala Mantra:
Oṃ sarvadharmagatānām amalamantrapadānāṃ svabhāvaśuddhānāṃ samayas tvam āḥ hūṃ.
Mountains of jewels, oceans of jewels, and exquisite jewel thrones; celestial garments, necklaces, wish-fulfilling trees,
jewel ponds, wondrous flowers, incense, lamps, and ointments— pervading the entire Dharma-realm and filling all of space,
these are the vast ocean of the self-nature of precious pearls, the most supreme among the seven treasures.
I now reverently present this offering of wondrous jewels gathered like clouds:
Mount Sumeru with its eight peaks at the center, the various forms of the four great continents,
surrounded by the sun and moon, gold, silver, and precious gems.
Musa-kha-’bab and lapis lazuli, Red pearls, and even emeralds and the like— I offer these before the Guru and the Triple Gem;
May you, out of compassion, graciously accept them! Oṃ sarvadharmaga-tara-dīpa-maha-mantra-pracaṭa.
*Mīkhasamvara-spharaṇasamaya āḥ hūṃ.* Relying now upon the instructions, I establish the maṇḍala;
its extent is equal to space, with vajras as its precious ground.
Each syllable is a secret mantra, accomplished through the mind alone, [forming] Mount Sumeru, the sun and moon, the seven treasures, and the four continents.
Clouds of robes, parasols, canopies, music, banners, and flags; Precious thrones, exquisite delicacies, pavilions, palaces, ponds, groves, and famous flowers are spread everywhere.
I offer these to the Guru, the Triple Gem, and the protective deities;
May you compassionately accept them with joy, dispel all demonic obstacles, and bestow merit and peace.
May all that the patrons seek this night be fulfilled as they wish; may auspiciousness continue without interruption throughout the bounds of the future.
Oṃ sarvadharmagatānāmahaṃ mantreṇa bhojaya me kha-samudra-spharaṇa-samayasvāhā hūṃ. (Ring the bell.)
At the altar, holding flowers and rice with the right hand, recite:

"I pray that the Guru and the Triple Gem, and the assembly of Buddhas within the maṇḍala, may compassionately accept and bestow their grace. May the merit and wisdom of the benefactor this day be fully adorned;

may all that is auspicious and favorable, both mundane and supramundane, be realized. May these benefits extend universally to all sentient beings throughout the entire dharmadhātu, so that they may swiftly [attain enlightenment]."
May I attain the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi. Namo Guru Vajra.

To propagate the Dharma is their domestic duty; they avoid the clamor of the dust and always sit in meditation in places of stillness and seclusion. May [obstacles] be warded off.

they first realize this realm and subsequently realize the realms of all Buddhas. Thus, Avalokiteśvara emits light.
The invocation of the Buddhas is like a practitioner invoking Avalokiteśvara;
here, one relies upon Avalokiteśvara to invite the Buddhas, for he is not the primary subject.

Praise to the Triple Gem:
To the World-Honored One, whose great compassion is wondrously adorned, who possesses perfect clarity and the wisdom of omniscience.
I pay homage to those who can bestow merit and wisdom like a great ocean, And to all Tathāgatas,
whose self-nature and essence are free from all desires; I pay homage to the wondrous Dharma,
which, by following this practice, Enables one to escape the evil realms through its profound and sublime principles.
Within the path of liberation, you possess supreme resolve; Upholding pure precepts and conduct, you are worthy of reverence;

On Potalaka he constantly enters meditative absorption; responding to conditions and manifesting to those who call upon him, there is nowhere his reach does not extend.

(The above constitutes making offerings to the Triple Gem, which is a gateway for cultivating merit. If one possesses merit but lacks wisdom, one will fall into the causal cycle of humans and devas;

Next, enter the meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) of Avalokiteśvara. The Master enters the concentration, and the Rector recites the verse. The sound should be valued for being gentle, harmonious, clear, and resonant;

When entering meditative absorption, close the eyes and clarify the mind. Visualize one’s own body as perfectly white and pure, like the bright moon.
Upon this pure lunar disc of the heart, visualize the syllable *Hrīḥ* emitting great radiance; this syllable transforms into an eight-petaled lotus.
Upon the flower is the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, with all physical marks and features clearly distinct, holding [an object] in his left hand.
A lotus flower. With his right hand, he makes the gesture of blossoming. He reflects thus:
"Within the bodies of all sentient beings, there exists this flower of awakening. It is the pure *dharmadhātu*, unstained by afflictions (*kleśa*). The lotus has eight petals;
upon each petal sits a Tathāgata in meditative equipoise (*samādhi*) with legs crossed, facing Avalokiteśvara, adorned with a halo around the neck, and his body like..."
Golden in color, its radiance dazzlingly brilliant. Visualize this eight-petaled lotus gradually unfolding and expanding until its magnitude equals the void.
With this awakened flower, illuminate and touch the ocean-like assembly of the Tathāgatas; may it become a vast offering (if the mind does not waver).
Within this meditative concentration, one generates profound compassion for infinite sentient beings.

Those who are touched by the illumination of these flowers of awakening are completely liberated from all suffering and affliction, becoming equal to Bodhisattvas in their physical marks and signs. Then, one should visualize the lotus flower gradually contracting.
Equal in measure to one's own body, one forms the mudrā and recites the mantra to empower four locations.

By means of this empowerment, the body is made firm—namely, the heart, forehead, throat, and crown. At each location marked by the mudrā, the syllable *hrīḥ* is formed. To form this syllable with the mudrā:
interlace the two hands with the palms facing outward, join the tips of the two index fingers like lotus petals, and extend the two thumbs upright side by side.
Then recite the mantra of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva (the Verse on the Samādhi of Avalokiteśvara):

I now vow to generate the bodhicitta.
I only pray that the Bodhisattva will come to take me under his care and swiftly realize the subtle and wondrous body of Avalokiteśvara,

(Commentary says: Next, one enters the *samādhi* that follows from the preceding and precedes the succeeding; this is the "auditory dust" [the object of hearing].

With a settled mind and eyes closed, one contemplates within the heart. (Commentary says: "With a settled mind" refers to the time of purity, when nothing is emitted internally. "Eyes closed" refers to the time of visualization, when external conditions do not enter. Question: The mind has no location; how can there be a "center"? Answer: It is said:

This clarifies the "flesh-ball mind" (*māṃsapiṇḍa-citta*). Because the mind of numinous awareness (*jñāna*) dwells within the flesh-ball mind, the Master should perform the six prohibitions at this point; this is a brief version of the reversal-verse (*pratiloma-gāthā*). Regarding its explanation:

one should visualize the syllable *baṅ* (𑖪) in red upon the tip of the heart. This transforms into an eight-petaled lotus of variegated colors. Upon the flower, one visualizes the white syllable *a* (अ), which transforms into a lunar disc (*candramaṇḍala*).
Upon the perfectly full, brilliant, and pure moon (Note:

"Perfectly full and brilliant" refers to the essence and function of the mind. Being "perfectly full," no virtue is lacking; this is the essence. Being "brilliant and pure," nothing is not illuminated; this is the function).
The Seed-Syllable *Hrīḥ* Emits Light and Becomes a Lotus (Note:

The seed-syllable is *hrīḥ*. This syllable is the principle by which the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion attains realization and the wondrous gateway for delivering sentient beings. Regarding "emitting light to become a lotus," this refers to the flower offered).
Within the flower is one Avalokiteśvara (the note states:

this refers to the *hrīḥ* heart-syllable increasing the self-body to become the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara; because he is unimpeded whether following or reversing [the flow of phenomena], he is called "Sovereign" (*īśvara*; the "flower" refers to the flower upon which he sits).
Endowed with the marks and signs of perfection, beyond compare (Note:

This is an abbreviation of a verse; its full explanation should state: one face, two arms, his body is golden in color, adorned with a floral crown and necklaces, wearing Amitābha Buddha upon his head—these are the words of praise for being beyond compare).
The left hand holds a wondrous lotus flower (the note says:
because principle can accomplish phenomena, it is said to "hold"; the flower symbolizes the simultaneity of cause and effect).
With the right hand, one makes the gesture of opening upon the leaf (the note says:
because phenomena can manifest principle, one is thus able to make the gesture of opening; all that precedes is self-awakening).
The Bodhisattva contemplates that the bodies of sentient beings each possess the lotus of awakening (Note:

These two lines constitute the awakening of others; they are called the conduct of a Bodhisattva. The meaning of the verse is that all sentient beings and Bodhisattvas are originally of one essence, for all possess the lotus of awakening; it is only due to delusion...)

Because they hold inverted attachments, they do not realize [the truth]. Therefore, the Bodhisattva contemplates them and gives rise to compassionate rescue. At this point, the practitioner must no longer conceive of the Bodhisattva and themselves as two separate entities.

Since previously one has already cultivated the visualization by increasing the seed-syllables, the "contemplation" mentioned here refers specifically to the words of the practitioner. If one cannot maintain such meditative concentration through mindful contemplation, then the methods practiced thus far will result in a mere waste of mental effort.
The pure dharma-realm is free from delusive defilement (Note:

This should be read as a single unit with the preceding two lines; it must not be split into two separate parts. Not even a speck of dust is established within the pure dharma-realm. It is stainless and pure. If one clings to this purity, it immediately becomes a defilement).
On each of the eight petals there is one Tathāgata (Note:

The "eight petals" refers to the eight petals of the lotus at the heart center. Regarding "each having one Tathāgata": the eight consciousnesses are originally one mind. Since they are one mind, they are identical to perfect enlightenment and constitute a single essence).

Therefore, it is said that they each exist as one. "One Tathāgata" refers to Avalokiteśvara. By saying "Tathāgata" rather than "Bodhisattva," it signifies a direct and transcendent arrival. These two phrases apply both to the perspective of others and to one's own.

From the perspective of others, it means that the minds of sentient beings are fundamentally pure and stainless, and that within the lotus flower there are eight Tathāgatas. From the perspective of oneself, it means that the practitioner enters meditative absorption simultaneously with the eight Tathāgatas.
The Tathāgatas enter meditative absorption and sit cross-legged, each facing Avalokiteśvara.

(Note: Question: There are many kinds of meditative absorptions. Which absorption does the Tathāgata enter now? Answer: It is the very absorption entered by the practitioner. This absorption is named the "Momentary Great Compassion Samādhi. Question again: Each...

Regarding the various faces: while the first four faces may be acceptable, how can the latter four faces not be considered "backed"? Answer: How could facing toward or away from anything be called the Tathāgata? This is precisely what is meant by the subtlety lying in the point of transformation. If one were to speak according to phenomenal characteristics:

The bodies of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are not like the segmented bodies of ordinary sentient beings; when facing east, they turn their backs to the west, and when facing south, they turn their backs to the north. The Bodhisattvas, however, are not thus. They possess the *manomaya-kāya* (mind-made body) that accords with the various classes of beings, manifesting transformations without fixed direction;

whether facing away or toward, all is correct. How could this be the case for the eight Tathāgatas? Or rather, whether it be a thousand or ten thousand Buddhas, there is no direction toward which they do not face correctly. Students should contemplate in this way, and furthermore, you must look into the place where there is neither facing nor turning away.
A halo encircles his neck, and his body is golden, its radiance shining brightly and brilliantly (Note:
The former phrase manifests his supreme body; the latter phrase manifests his supreme environment).
Next, visualize that the flowers gradually unfold and expand in magnitude until they pervade the entire realm of empty space. (Note:

The preceding seven lines and fourteen verses all manifest the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Now, with these two lines, one enters the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena. "Next, visualize" refers to the time of practice. By grasping phenomena...)

Because it is established by principle, it can gradually expand and become vast; because principle conforms to the transformations of phenomena, it can pervade the entire Dharma-realm, such that its vastness has no exterior. All of this is the realm of Mind-only; it is not a matter external to the mind.
Contemplate that the flowers of awakening illuminate the Dharma-realm, co-extensive with the vast assembly of Tathāgatas. (Note:

These two lines precisely clarify the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena. "Flowers of awakening" is a phenomenon; "the assembly of the ocean" is also a phenomenon. When the flowers of awakening pervade all time, they are simultaneous with the vast assembly of Tathāgatas, being expansive and without limit.)

Obstruction. It is like a thousand lamps in a single room; though their lights intermingle, they do not become confused. The "Dharma-realm" refers to the ten Dharma-realms, which comprise the four noble realms and the six ordinary realms. The meaning is that when these flowers unfold and expand, they are able to illuminate these ten Dharma-realms.
It is identical to the one true reality, with no further distinction.
If the mind does not shift from this,
it will surely have compassion for all sentient beings.

(Commentary states: The upper phrase refers to self-awakening; the lower phrase refers to awakening others. What has preceded—contemplating sentient beings—is the initial arousal of practice. Reaching this point of pitying all beings is the actualization of that practice.
This means that only by realizing this unimpeded, vast realm can one truly engage in practice to deliver sentient beings. There is profound mystery herein; students must not fail to be cautious.)
The flower of awakening, having received this illumination,
is freed from suffering and affliction (the note says: this is the efficacy of benefiting sentient beings),
and thus becomes identical to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
(Commentary states: This refers to the fruit obtained; it means that at the very moment of first generating the resolve, one immediately attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.)

The lotus gradually withdraws to the same measure as itself. (Note: The preceding eight lines all expand; this one line alone contracts. According to the Esoteric [teaching], this is the ultimate increase. As Lūyipāda’s *Pratyakṣa* explains: "Arising from the state of correctness is called 'increase';

returning to the state of correctness is the 'ultimate. This is also the non-duality of the beginning and the source. The Guru said: "To emit without withdrawing is like an ordinary person; to withdraw without emitting is called a Śrāvaka; to both withdraw and emit is called the Secret [Vehicle]."

Regarding the "sphere" (*viṣaya*): when both gathering and releasing are entirely unnecessary, it is called "the absence of conceptual proliferation" (*niṣprapañca*). This is the most ultimate *mūlatantra*. One must not fail to realize how easily the single word "gathering" has been circulated; students, moreover, should not regard this as a matter of ordinary hearing or seeing.
Furthermore, bind the seal of the Sovereign Avalokiteśvara, empower the four places, and recite the mantra (Note:

These two phrases both refer to the practitioner, who requests the hidden power of the Wisdom Buddha for assistance. As for the "mantra," this refers to the secret mantras of the hand seals that follow).

"One observes oneself as equal to Avalokiteśvara" (Note: Regarding "turning the light back to reflect": since one has previously observed Avalokiteśvara, there is now a concern that one might become deluded and pursue external objects; thus, one turns back to observe one's own body, hence it is said "also equal. Now, for what reason is it further stated "also equal"?

Having already increased through the seed-syllables so as to become Avalokiteśvara, why is it again called "also equal"? The answer is: the initial increase occurred because one had not yet transcended conceptualization (*buddhi*); this present state, however, is the ground of ultimate reality, which is direct realization and direct entry.)

It is like Sudhana’s first meeting with Mañjuśrī and the others. Furthermore, the previously visualized Avalokiteśvara, when viewed from the perspective of the cause, is called "the fruit within the cause. After the empowerment through secret mantras (*dhāraṇī*), it is the "cause within the fruit" in its essential nature. One might ask:

"Since one has already entered the maṇḍala and immediately given rise to the pride (*māna*) of being Avalokiteśvara, why does one now again enter this samādhi? Is this not redundant? No, it is not so. The former was the fundamental samādhi; it is also called the "correct position" (*samyag-sthāna*) and the "correct essence" (*samyag-ātman*).

It is like a person living as a householder. The samādhi entered subsequently is the "samādhi of activity. It is like that same person serving as a minister in the state. In reality, they are of one essence, though they differ according to their location. It is also like a person who, when at court, is part of the court...

Regarding clothing: when among the military, one wears military attire. Thus, in the fundamental concentration (*mauladhyāna*), the color is white; in the concentration of application (*prayogadhyāna*), it is golden. Below these, according to each successive ritual procedure, there are many changes in the color of the body. One should always examine matters through this principle; therefore, do not harbor doubts regarding these various [appearances].
By means of these supreme merits of meditative concentration,
I dedicate them so that all sentient beings throughout the dharma realm may together behold the Western Land of Immeasurable Light and accomplish the vast vows of Samantabhadra. Oṃ vajratrama hṛīḥ.

(Bind the Avalokiteśvara Seal of Sovereignty. With the two hands joined palm-to-palm externally, the two index fingers touch one another like lotus petals, and the two thumbs are held upright side-by-side.
While reciting the mantra, empower the four places—the crown of the head, the throat, the heart, and the navel.
The Master’s seal and mantra may be known [from the ritual manual]. At each location, press with the hand seal and recite the mantra once. Furthermore, with...)
Empower with the syllable Oṃ and place the mudrā upon the mouth. Next, empower the crown of the head with the syllable Hūṃ.
Empower the navel with the syllable Raṃ (raṃ). Empower the heart with the syllable Hrīḥ (hrīḥ). Empower the throat with the syllable A.
By means of this empowerment, the body is made firm and solid; therefore, no demonic obstacles whatsoever can cause harm.
(The attendant said:)
If a person wishes to fully understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, they should contemplate that the nature of the dharma-realm is entirely created by mind alone.

Immediately, form the seal for destroying hell (with both hands in vajra-fists, the two wisdom fingers hooking together, and the two thumbs extended and supporting each other; recite three times and strike three times to destroy hell).
NAMAḤ AṢṬĀṢṬA-CETIṆĀM SAMYAKSAṂBUDDHA-KOṬINĀM | OṂ CULA CULA VAPOṢE TIRI TIRI HŪṂ ||
(The Master’s seal-mantra may be understood from the source. One should visualize oneself as the increasing red Avalokiteśvara, with one face and two arms.
At the three locations—the tongue, the heart center, and upon the seal—there is a red syllable *hrīḥ*, emitting light that is red like the radiance of the newly risen sun.
This light shines upon and touches the hells, completely destroying them all. A question is asked: "Does it emit [light] from a single location...")
Question: The light alone is sufficient to destroy it; why employ all three? Answer:
Because that hell is created by the three karmas of sentient beings, we now likewise employ the three karmas to emit light and destroy it. Question again:
Since hell is formed by the individual karma of sentient beings, how can it be destroyed? Answer: Although it is said to be individual karma, it is nonetheless of one and the same mind.
Illuminating this with wisdom, one sees that sentient beings do not exist; how, then, could there be hells?
It is because of delusion regarding the One Mind that one falsely creates various evils. When these evil karmas ripen, one falsely manifests hells.

Having fallen into hell, one falsely perceives the experience of suffering—just as in a dream one may be devoured by tigers, wolves, or lions, or bound by bandits, or encounter royal calamities and undergo various [torments].
Suffering. Yet upon waking from the dream, nothing at all is found. Why is this? Because in reality, no such things exist within the dream.
Now, observing the hells and their sufferings, it is likewise so. One must now certainly shatter them through the power of the illumination of wisdom. Question:
Since the hells are fundamentally empty in this way, why is it necessary to shatter them in order to save those beings? Answer: Although I—through [the power of wisdom]...
The power of wisdom-illumination knows that their origin is empty; they lack such wisdom-illumination, so how could they not suffer? Thus, the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* says:
"While dreaming, it is not non-existent, yet upon waking, nothing at all can be found. Now, to rescue them, one precisely intends to shatter this hell and its suffering-emptiness.
If one traces the matter back to its source, they have come to form this hell through the causal conditions of their own evil karma.
Thus one knows that [suffering] is not inherently existent. I now employ wisdom to illuminate the causes and conditions to dismantle it; how could this not be a dismantling?
First is meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), second is hand-seals (*mudrā*), third is mantra (*mantra*), fourth is visualization (*bhāvanā*), and fifth is the illumination of wisdom.
With these five kinds of causes and conditions, what task would not be accomplished? How could it be limited merely to the destruction of hell? As for the scholars of the present age, they...
Seeking only profit, they arrogantly assume the title of *ācārya* and act as leaders of the assembly;
yet while they ring bells and beat cymbals to the rhythm, there are many who fear they may fail to fulfill the intentions of their patrons. Should one not be cautious?

By the power of the majestic spiritual authority of this mudrā and mantra, all the gates to the hells within the various realms of existence shall open wide of their own accord in accordance with this mudrā and mantra.
We reverently invoke the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha (the Director raises the incense and flowers to welcome him; having completed the invocation, the leader holds the censer and says):
Homage! With single-minded devotion, we reverently invite you: Only when all sentient beings have been delivered will you realize Bodhi;
until hell is emptied, you vow not to become a Buddha. Great Holy Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, we pray that you do not violate your original vow.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, you have graced this Dharma assembly with your presence this very night.

We invite you with incense and flowers. *Namo*, with a single mind we respectfully invite you. Your face is like indigo; your hair is like vermilion. Your form is like mountains and oceans; your neck is like—
Needle. A moving broken cart; its sound is like a roar. We now invite the Great Being Mārana and the Ghost King Yankou.
We pray that you will act as our uninvited friend, exercising unconditional compassion, and grace this Dharma assembly at this very moment tonight (with incense and flowers).

Homage! With single-minded devotion, we respectfully invite you. You who entered meditative absorption in the forest and sat peacefully upon your dhyāna-seat, before whom the realm of hungry ghosts cried out from their hunger and emptiness, and from whom the roots of existence for beings in the realms of darkness and light, water and land, sprang forth;

you who overturned the banner of the teaching for the sake of the Second Patriarch—now we invite the Great Being, the Venerable Ānanda, to open the gates of the Dharma. We pray that you emerge from samādhi and employ your six supernormal powers this very night.
At that time, the light descends upon the Dharma assembly.

(The assembly unites in offering incense and flowers; the Master places them in the incense burner, performs the four *cakra-mudrās*, recites *jaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ*, forms the mudrā while silently reciting, and extends the five offerings.)

With single-minded devotion we offer this invocation. Through the resonance of the five supernatural powers, the One Nature remains unimpaired. You conduct yourselves with integrity among humanity and spread wisdom throughout the world.
We now invoke the gods of the city walls and moats of this prefecture, the presiding local deities of this region, together with all your subordinate hosts.
We pray that you will above obey the Buddha’s command and below have compassion for the sentiments of ordinary beings. At this very hour of this night:
You have graced this Dharma assembly with your presence.

We invoke you with single-minded devotion: holding banners and canopies in hand, draped in floral curtains, you guide sentient beings to the Land of Ultimate Bliss and lead the deceased to attend this gathering at the site of practice.
Now we invite the King-Bodhisattva Who Leads Souls on the Path to the Netherworld.
O Mahāsattva, we pray that you do not violate your original vow; out of compassion for sentient beings, please come to this Dharma assembly at this very hour tonight.

We invoke you with single-minded devotion: from the ten-thousand-fathom depths of the Jade Pond, the golden breeze stirs and causes lotuses to bloom upon the water; from the thousand-tiered jeweled pavilion, [you descend].
As the pearl curtains were rolled up, the Buddha was seen amidst the clouds;
[the deceased] returned his devotion to the Triple Gem. To celebrate this birth and repay their kindness, a vegetarian feast and food offerings were prepared.

[I], disciple [Name], have reverently invited the Vajra Master on this night to perform the Yoga-Yamantaka *Ullambana* ritual for the distribution of food. Taking this virtuous cause as the beginning, I now burn this named incense.
First, the invocation is extended. We invoke the deceased [Name], who has passed away during this fast.
We pray that, by the power of the Triple Gem and relying upon secret mantras, you will come at this very moment tonight to receive this unobstructed feast of ambrosia.
With single-minded devotion, I invoke you. Lu Yi’s prescriptions for longevity are but empty talk; the magpie’s boast of an elixir of immortality is in vain.
Even the sun and moon suffer eclipses; among those who dwell in the human realm, who is not subject to impermanence?
I offer this back to the Triple Gem (as stated previously, etc.).
With single-minded devotion, I invoke you. The vast and boundless waves of the Nine Rivers surge; the celestial music of the Nine Heavens comes to welcome you.
Within the radiance of the Nine Palaces, I behold the Tathāgata. May the ancestors who have passed away be reborn in the Buddha-realm.
I now offer this back to the Triple Gem (as before, etc.).

With single-minded devotion, I invoke the sovereign emperors of successive dynasties and the feudal lords and kings of past ages, who dwell loftily within the nine-layered palace halls and alone command the ten-thousand-li mountains and rivers.

The cries of grievance from the five kingdoms have not yet ceased. (Alas! The cuckoo calls as it brings down the peach blossoms of the moon;
blood stains the branches, and the sorrow remains ever long. Such are the former kings and later lords, along with the various classes of the *jinling* spirits and other multitudes.
